# The Komlos-Sulyok-Szemeredi bound: every finite set of reals has a Sidon subset of size c sqrt n


Call a set of reals a *Sidon set* when all its pairwise sums are distinct: if $a + b = c + d$ with all four in the set, then $\{a,b\} = \{c,d\}$.

We want an absolute constant $c > 0$ such that every finite set $X$ of positive reals contains a Sidon subset $S$ with $|S| \ge c\sqrt{|X|}$.

This is the lower bound half of [Erdos problem 530](https://www.erdosproblems.com/530), posed by Riddell. The right constant is still unknown. Erdos observed the matching $(1+o(1))N^{1/2}$ upper bound from $A = \{1, \dots, N\}$. Komlos, Sulyok, and Szemeredi settled the order in 1975, as a case of a general theorem about linear equations. Their paper is *Linear problems in combinatorial number theory*, Acta Math. Acad. Sci. Hungar. 26 (1975) 113-121 (doi 10.1007/BF01895954). Bailleul and Riblet give a much shorter proof in [arXiv:2605.03181](https://arxiv.org/abs/2605.03181).

## The cube root

Maximality alone gives $|S| \ge c|X|^{1/3}$. Take a Sidon subset $S$ of maximum size. Every $x$ outside it satisfies $x = s + t - r$ or $x = (s+t)/2$ for some $r, s, t \in S$, so $|X| \le 3|S|^3$.

## The shared idea

Compress, then pigeonhole against a known Sidon set.

First move the reals into $\mathbb{Z}$. A finite set spans a finite dimensional $\mathbb{Q}$-vector space, and a generic rational functional separates its points while preserving every relation $a + b = c + d$. Then squeeze the integers into an interval of length comparable to their number, keeping a constant fraction and keeping Sidon subsets liftable. Finally, intersect with a translate of the Erdos-Turan set, which has about $\sqrt{N}$ elements inside $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$. A set of size $\Theta(n)$ inside $[1,n]$ meets some translate of a Sidon set of size $\sqrt{n}$ in order $\sqrt{n}$ points.

## The two routes

The proofs differ only in how they compress. The mission has the 2026 route in full, and the 1975 route without its first range reduction, Lemma 2. The 1975 route uses Lemmas 3, 4, and 5, all built on the small remainder map of Remark 3. Finding its modulus needs a prime counting bound. The 2026 route replaces them with one averaging lemma over a real rotation parameter $\theta$.

## Formalization choices

The Sidon condition, the Erdos-Turan set, and the 1975 reduction relation are written out at each use.

The 2026 paper finishes with Singer's 1938 covering of $\mathbb{Z}/(q^2+q+1)\mathbb{Z}$ by $q+1$ Sidon sets. Mathlib doesn't have perfect difference sets, so we average over translates instead. That gives the same order and a worse constant, which is fine since the goal only asks for some $c > 0$.

Lemmas 2 and 6 of the 1975 paper are missing on purpose. Our formalizations of both turned out false, so we dropped them. The 2026 route doesn't need them, or Lemma 1'.

## Bailleul-Riblet Lemma 2.3: compression by a real rotation parameter


For a finite integer set $A$ and positive $m$, some subset $C$ of $A$ with at least $|A|/2 - |A|^2/(2m)$ elements maps injectively into $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$, preserving $a + b = c + d$.

Put $\varphi_\theta(a) = \lfloor am\theta \rfloor \bmod m$ and keep $B_\theta = \{a \in A : \{am\theta\} < 1/2\}$. On $B_\theta$ two fractional parts sum to less than one, so no carry occurs and $\varphi_\theta$ is additive. Multiplication by a nonzero integer preserves Lebesgue measure mod one, so $|B_\theta|$ averages at least $|A|/2$ over $\theta \in [0,1)$. Each colliding pair costs at most $1/m$ on average. Choose a $\theta$ beating both averages, then delete one element from each colliding pair.

## The Erdos-Turan set has exactly $p$ elements


The set $\{2pk + (k^2 \bmod p) : 0 \le k < p\}$ has exactly $p$ elements.

Since $k^2 \bmod p$ is below $p$, the value $2pk + (k^2 \bmod p)$ determines $k$ as its quotient by $2p$.

## The Erdos-Turan set lives below $2p^2$


Every element of $\{2pk + (k^2 \bmod p) : 0 \le k < p\}$ is less than $2p^2$, since the largest is at most $2p(p-1) + (p-1) = 2p^2 - p - 1$.

## The Erdos-Turan set is Sidon, for $p$ prime


All pairwise sums of $\{2pk + (k^2 \bmod p) : 0 \le k < p\}$ are distinct when $p$ is prime.

Write the four elements as $2pk_i + r_i$ with $r_i = k_i^2 \bmod p$. Each $r_i$ is below $p$, so $r_1 + r_2 < 2p$ and $r_3 + r_4 < 2p$. Uniqueness of quotient and remainder modulo $2p$ splits $a_1 + a_2 = a_3 + a_4$ into $k_1 + k_2 = k_3 + k_4$ and $r_1 + r_2 = r_3 + r_4$. The second reads $k_1^2 + k_2^2 \equiv k_3^2 + k_4^2 \pmod p$. So the pairs have equal sum and equal product, and they're the roots of the same quadratic over the field $\mathbb{F}_p$. (This needs $p$ odd. At $p = 2$ the set is $\{0, 5\}$, which is Sidon.)

The construction fails at composite $p$ such as 4, 6, 8, 9, and 10, where $\mathbb{Z}/p\mathbb{Z}$ isn't a field.

## An integer-valued Freiman 2-embedding of a finite set of reals


For every finite set $X$ of reals, some map $\varphi$ from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{Z}$ is injective on $X$ and preserves $a + b = c + d$ on $X$.

Clear denominators in the rational functional that is injective on $X$. One common denominator sends it into $\mathbb{Z}$ on $X$, and scaling keeps it linear.

## Lemma 3: the second range reduction, down to $n^{3/2}$


Any $n$ positive integers bounded by $M$, with $M \le n^3$, reduce to a Sidon-faithful set of at least $cn$ positive integers $b$ with $b^2 \le n^3$. Here $c > 0$ is absolute.

*Sidon-faithful* means $A$ reduces to $B$: every Sidon subset of $B$ is matched by a Sidon subset of $A$ at least as large. So a lower bound proved for $B$ transfers back to $A$.

The squared bound says $b \le n^{3/2}$ without leaving $\mathbb{Z}$.

## Lemma 4: the third range reduction, down to $n$


For some absolute $c > 0$, any $n$ positive integers bounded by $n^{3/2}$ reduce to a Sidon-faithful set of at least $cn$ positive integers bounded by $n$.

The paper's bound $3n/\alpha$, with $\alpha = 4$ for the Sidon relation, is $3n/4$ here, below $n$.

## Lemma 5: any $n$ positive integers compress into $[1, n]$


For some absolute $c > 0$, any $n$ positive integers reduce to a Sidon-faithful set of at least $cn$ positive integers all at most $n$.

The paper's constant is $1/(4\alpha^6)$, which is $1/16384$ with $\alpha = 4$ for the Sidon relation. We left the constant existential because we read that numeral off a poor scan of the paper. A slightly too strong constant would be unprovable.

## Maximality forces $|X| \le 3|S|^3$


If $S$ is a Sidon subset of $X$ of maximum size, then $|X| \le 3|S|^3$.

Adding any $x$ outside $S$ breaks the Sidon property, so some relation involves $x$. Either $x + b = c + d$ with $b, c, d \in S$, so $x = c + d - b$, at most $|S|^3$ values. Or $x + x = c + d$, so $x = (c+d)/2$, at most $|S|^2$ values. That gives $|X| \le |S| + |S|^2 + |S|^3 \le 3|S|^3$, using $|S| \ge 1$ when $X$ is nonempty.

## A Sidon subset of maximum cardinality exists


Every finite set of reals has a Sidon subset no smaller than any other Sidon subset.

A finite set has finitely many subsets, and the empty set is always Sidon, so a largest Sidon subset exists.

## A $\mathbb{Q}$-linear functional injective on a finite set of reals


For every finite set $X$ of reals there is a $\mathbb{Q}$-linear map from $\mathbb{R}$ to $\mathbb{Q}$ that is injective on $X$.

Pick a basis of the $\mathbb{Q}$-span of $X$ and clear denominators in the coordinates. Then read the integer coordinate vectors in base $M$, for $M$ past every coordinate difference. Extending to all of $\mathbb{R}$ takes a Hamel basis.

## Remark 3: a small remainder map preserves $a+b=c+d$


If every $a$ in $A$ is written $a = k(a)q + r(a)$ with $4|r(a)| < q$, then $a \mapsto r(a)$ preserves the relation $a + b = c + d$.

Each remainder sum has absolute value below $q/2$, so their difference is a multiple of $q$ with absolute value below $q$, hence zero.

The 4 is the paper's $\alpha$ for the coefficient vector $(1, 1, -1, -1)$ of the Sidon relation.

## The cube-root bound: a Sidon subset of size $c|X|^{1/3}$


There is an absolute $c > 0$ such that every finite set of reals has a Sidon subset of size at least $c|X|^{1/3}$. It follows with $c = 3^{-1/3}$, because a maximum Sidon subset exists and maximality forces $|X| \le 3|S|^3$.

## A Sidon subset of $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ of size at least $\sqrt{N}/4$


For every $N$ there is a Sidon set inside $\{0, \dots, N-1\}$ with at least $\sqrt{N}/4$ elements.

For $N \le 144$ the set $\{0, 1, 3\}$ has three elements and $\sqrt{144}/4 = 3$, and for $N < 4$ at most one element is needed. For $N > 144$, take $m = \lfloor\sqrt{N/2}\rfloor/2$ and use Bertrand's postulate to get a prime $p$ with $m < p \le 2m$. Then $2p^2 \le N$. The Erdos-Turan set lives below $2p^2$, so it sits inside the interval, and $p > m$ beats $\sqrt{N}/4$.

## The Komlos-Sulyok-Szemeredi bound: a Sidon subset of size $c\sqrt{|X|}$


For some absolute constant $c > 0$, every finite set $X$ of positive reals contains a subset $S$ with distinct pairwise sums and $|S| \ge c\sqrt{|X|}$.

Such an $S$ is a *Sidon set*: for $w, x, y, z \in S$ with $w + x = y + z$, either $w = y$ and $x = z$, or $w = z$ and $x = y$. Repeats are allowed, so $w = x$ is fine.

The constant comes before the $\forall X$, so it must handle small $X$ too, which a one-element Sidon set does. Positivity is never used, since the Sidon condition is translation invariant.

## Pull a Sidon set back from the integer image


Given $\varphi$ injective on $X$ and preserving $a + b = c + d$, every Sidon subset $T$ of $\varphi(X)$ has a Sidon preimage in $X$ at least as large.

Only this direction is ever needed, so the embedding preserves the relation and doesn't have to reflect it.

## Some translate of $B$ meets $A$ in $|A||B|/m$ points


For $A$ and $B$ inside $\mathbb{Z}/m\mathbb{Z}$, some translate $B + i$ meets $A$ in at least $|A||B|/m$ points, by double counting over all $m$ translates.

This replaces the published proof's covering of $\mathbb{Z}/(q^2+q+1)\mathbb{Z}$ by $q+1$ Sidon sets. A Sidon set of size about $\sqrt{m}$ meets a set of size $s$ in about $s/\sqrt{m}$ points, the same order. Singer's constant $1/(3\sqrt{3})$ is better, but the goal only needs some $c > 0$.
